item.title: How Fast Does the ISS Travel? Speed in mph, km/h, and m/s

item.description: Over 9,000 active satellites orbit Earth in 2026. Plus 30,000+ pieces of trackable debris. Get the latest numbers, who operates them, and why the count keeps growing.

item.title: Why Do Astronauts Float in Space? (Microgravity Explained)
item.description: Astronauts float because they're in free fall—constantly falling toward Earth but moving fast enough to miss it. It's not zero gravity. Simple explanation for kids and students.

item.title: What Happens If You Fall Into a Black Hole?
item.description: Black holes are among the most mysterious objects in the universe. Learn what a black hole is, what scientists predict would happen if you fell in, and why NASA studies them.

item.title: How the ISS Orbits Earth 16 Times Every Day
item.description: The International Space Station completes one orbit every 90 minutes, meaning astronauts see 16 sunrises and sunsets in a single day. Learn why this happens and how orbital mechanics make it possible.

item.title: James Webb Telescope: Latest Discoveries in 2026
item.description: The James Webb Space Telescope continues to revolutionize astronomy. Latest findings include ancient galaxies, exoplanet atmospheres, and insights into star formation.

item.title: What is Geostationary Orbit? Explained Simply
item.description: Geostationary satellites appear to stay fixed in the sky. Learn why they orbit at exactly 35,786 km, how they're used for TV and weather, and the physics behind this special orbit.

item.title: Why Satellites Don't Fall: Gravity and Velocity Explained
item.description: Satellites don't fall because they're moving fast enough sideways that they keep missing Earth. Learn the physics behind orbital motion and why speed matters.
